title: Esther 8:1–8
context: Haman has been hanged (7:10), but his decree to destroy the Jews on the thirteenth day of Adar still stands (3:12–13). The king gives Haman’s house to Esther, and his signet ring to Mordecai, whom Esther sets over Haman’s house. Esther again risks approaching the king, falls at his feet in tears, and asks that Haman’s letters be reversed. The king explains that a decree written in the king’s name and sealed with his ring cannot be revoked, and authorizes Esther and Mordecai to write a new decree as they see fit (8:8). The book of Esther never names God. Readers in both traditions commonly see God’s hidden providence in the reversals of the story, and that reading is shared ground, but the narrator states only what the people do and what happens. Both traditions read the unit as shared ground about courageous intercession for one’s people and about the limits of human power.

verses.text: On that day, King Ahasuerus gave the house of Haman, the Jews’ enemy, to Esther the queen. Mordecai came before the king; for Esther had told what he was to her.
verses.arminianNotes: The king gives Haman’s house to Esther, and Mordecai comes before the king because Esther has told him their relationship. Arminian readers note the dramatic reversal: the enemy’s property passes to the one he sought to destroy, and Esther’s honesty opens the way for Mordecai.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a striking reversal and, with many readers, discern God’s hidden providence behind it, though the book does not name God. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the turning of fortunes the story has been building toward, without decoding every detail.

verses.text: The king took off his ring, which he had taken from Haman, and gave it to Mordecai. Esther set Mordecai over the house of Haman.
verses.arminianNotes: The king gives Mordecai the ring he took from Haman, and Esther sets Mordecai over Haman’s house. Arminian readers note that authority once used for evil now passes to a man who will use it to protect his people. Responsibility comes with the ring.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the transfer of power as part of the story’s great reversal. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that the means of Haman’s plot (3:10) now pass to Mordecai, and both see in it a sign of deliverance still to be completed.

verses.text: Esther spoke yet again before the king, and fell down at his feet and begged him with tears to put away the mischief of Haman the Agagite, and his plan that he had planned against the Jews.
verses.arminianNotes: Esther speaks again, falls at the king’s feet, and begs with tears that Haman’s plan against the Jews be put away. Arminian readers note that her personal safety is not enough for her; she risks herself again for her people. Her intercession is costly and sincere.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Esther’s courage and compassion as a model of intercession. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that Haman’s death has not removed the danger, and that Esther rightly continues to plead for her people rather than resting in her own security.

verses.text: Then the king held out to Esther the golden scepter. So Esther arose, and stood before the king.
verses.arminianNotes: The king holds out the golden scepter, and Esther rises and stands before him. Arminian readers note that the gesture grants her a hearing, as in 5:2. Her willingness to approach the king again is met with favor, and she is able to make her request.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the king’s favor as the door through which Esther’s petition can be heard, and many discern God’s hidden care in that favor, though the text does not say so. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a moment of grace extended to a courageous intercessor.

verses.text: She said, “If it pleases the king, and if I have found favor in his sight, and the thing seems right to the king, and I am pleasing in his eyes, let it be written to reverse the letters devised by Haman, the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, which he wrote to destroy the Jews who are in all the king’s provinces.
verses.arminianNotes: Esther asks, with careful courtesy, that letters be written to reverse Haman’s decree to destroy the Jews. Arminian readers note her wisdom in framing the request to please the king. Courage and tact work together in her appeal for her people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note her skillful appeal and her naming of Haman as the author of the plot. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an example of wise and persistent advocacy, and both see Esther using her position responsibly for the good of others.

verses.text: For how can I endure to see the evil that would come to my people? How can I endure to see the destruction of my relatives?”
verses.arminianNotes: “For how can I endure to see the evil that would come to my people?” Arminian readers hear deep personal grief and solidarity. Esther identifies fully with her relatives and cannot accept her own safety while they face destruction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear love for her people and see in it a reflection of the compassion God’s servants should have for others. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the heart of Esther’s appeal, showing that true leadership feels the suffering of those it represents.

verses.text: Then King Ahasuerus said to Esther the queen and to Mordecai the Jew, “See, I have given Esther the house of Haman, and they have hanged him on the gallows because he laid his hand on the Jews.
verses.arminianNotes: The king reminds Esther and Mordecai that he has given them Haman’s house and that Haman was hanged “because he laid his hand on the Jews.” Arminian readers note the king’s recognition that Haman’s plot was wrong. Justice has begun, though the danger remains.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the king’s acknowledgment of Haman’s guilt and the partial reversal already accomplished. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the king affirming what he has done while preparing to give Esther and Mordecai authority to act further.

verses.text: Write also to the Jews as it pleases you, in the king’s name, and seal it with the king’s ring; for the writing which is written in the king’s name, and sealed with the king’s ring, may not be reversed by any man.”
verses.arminianNotes: The king authorizes them to write as they please in his name, since a sealed royal decree cannot be revoked. Arminian readers note the limits of human power: even the king cannot undo his own law, so a new decree must answer the old one.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the irrevocable law (compare 1:19) and the need for a counter-decree. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing the inflexibility of human law and the responsibility now placed on Esther and Mordecai to protect their people within it.
